title: t12 Neural networks and deep learning — narration (English)

items.title: Remember our two-knob taxi-fare machine?
items.subtitle: Remember our two-knob taxi-fare machine? It learned how fares change with distance just fine.

items.title: But fares also depend on the time of day:
items.subtitle: But fares also depend on the time of day: rush hour costs more, and late night a little more too.

items.title: It can't learn that
items.subtitle: It can't learn that, because all it can draw is a straight line.

items.title: So how does a machine
items.subtitle: So how does a machine learn a pattern that bends? With a neural network.

items.title: Last time, turning the knobs was like
items.subtitle: Last time, turning the knobs was like walking downhill blindfolded, always stepping where the score drops fastest.

items.title: Today we'll build a tiny
items.subtitle: Today we'll build a tiny network that learns the bend, see why more layers help, and meet AlexNet.

items.title: Here's some made-up data:
items.subtitle: Here's some made-up data: the same 5-kilometer ride, 48 times, at different hours of the day.

items.title: Daytime rides cost about $23
items.subtitle: Daytime rides cost about $23, just what our two-knob machine charges.

items.title: Around 8 a.m.
items.subtitle: Around 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. it spikes, and late at night it's a bit pricier.

items.title: Same two knobs
items.subtitle: Same two knobs, one for height and one for slope, but now we feed it the time, not the distance.

items.title: However you turn them
items.subtitle: However you turn them, the best you get is a nearly flat line through the middle.

items.title: It undercharges at rush
items.subtitle: It undercharges at rush hour and overcharges by day. Its loss, the score for how wrong it is, can't get below 11.5.

items.title: The knobs aren't the problem:
items.subtitle: The knobs aren't the problem: this machine only draws straight lines, and the pattern bends.

items.title: The fix isn't one big machine.
items.subtitle: The fix isn't one big machine. It's lots of simple little ones.

items.title: Each unit still has two
items.subtitle: Each unit still has two knobs and draws a line, plus one rule: anything below zero becomes zero.

items.title: Its line stays flat, then bends upward.
items.subtitle: Its line stays flat, then bends upward.

items.title: The two knobs set where
items.subtitle: The two knobs set where it bends and how steep it gets.

items.title: One bend isn't enough
items.subtitle: One bend isn't enough, so add more units that bend in different spots.

items.title: Add them up, and you can build bumps
items.subtitle: Add them up, and you can build bumps, steps, almost any curve.

items.title: Our network has 12 units side
items.subtitle: Our network has 12 units side by side in the first layer, and one unit in the second.

items.title: That unit scales each
items.subtitle: That unit scales each bent line with a knob, adds them up, then one last knob shifts the total. That's the fare.

items.title: Thirty-seven knobs in all.
items.subtitle: Thirty-seven knobs in all.

items.title: Layers of little units like
items.subtitle: Layers of little units like this are what we call a neural network.

items.title: The name comes from neurons in the brain
items.subtitle: The name comes from neurons in the brain, but don't take that too seriously.

items.title: To turn all thirty-seven
items.subtitle: To turn all thirty-seven, we use last episode's trick, nudging every knob whichever way drops the loss fastest.

items.title: Our curve starts as a random squiggle
items.subtitle: Our curve starts as a random squiggle, and step by step it bends toward the peaks.

items.title: After 10,000 steps
items.subtitle: After 10,000 steps, the loss is down to 0.26. The best straight line never got below 11.5.

items.title: Rush hours and late nights
items.subtitle: Rush hours and late nights, it catches them all.

items.title: And every corner on this curve
items.subtitle: And every corner on this curve is one little unit making its bend.

items.title: By the way
items.subtitle: By the way, there's a much faster trick for finding which way to turn each knob. More on that next time.

items.title: So far, we've put units side by side
items.subtitle: So far, we've put units side by side, each adding one bend.

items.title: Now stack them
items.subtitle: Now stack them, so each layer folds the line it gets from the layer before, like folding paper.

items.title: For example, two units per layer can fold
items.subtitle: For example, two units per layer can fold a slanted line exactly in half.

items.title: One layer makes two straight pieces
items.subtitle: One layer makes two straight pieces, two layers make four, and in this example each new layer doubles that.

items.title: So ten units side by side
items.subtitle: So ten units side by side give at most 11 pieces. Stacked five deep, they can give 32.

items.title: Later layers reuse what
items.subtitle: Later layers reuse what earlier ones already folded.

items.title: The deeper the stack
items.subtitle: The deeper the stack, the more complex the shapes the same units can build.

items.title: That's the "deep" in deep learning.
items.subtitle: That's the "deep" in deep learning.

items.title: In 2012, three researchers at the University
items.subtitle: In 2012, three researchers at the University of Toronto trained a very deep neural network.

items.title: Their network became known as AlexNet.
items.subtitle: Their network became known as AlexNet.

items.title: It had 8 layers and 60 million knobs.
items.subtitle: It had 8 layers and 60 million knobs. It learned 1,000 categories from 1.2 million photos.

items.title: At that year's ImageNet contest
items.subtitle: At that year's ImageNet contest, it got five guesses per picture, and only missed if all five were wrong.

items.title: The version they entered got 15.3% wrong.
items.subtitle: The version they entered got 15.3% wrong. The runner-up got 26.2%.

items.title: Nobody told it what to look for
items.subtitle: Nobody told it what to look for, yet its first layer learned to spot stripes at every angle, and patches of color.

items.title: Later layers combined those into
items.subtitle: Later layers combined those into more and more complex patterns.

items.title: Removing any middle layer made
items.subtitle: Removing any middle layer made its first-guess accuracy drop about 2 percentage points.

items.title: As the paper put it
items.subtitle: As the paper put it, "the depth really is important."

items.title: So a neural network is just
items.subtitle: So a neural network is just simple little units with knobs, stacked layer on layer.

items.title: Stack them deep enough
items.subtitle: Stack them deep enough, and they can recognize really complicated things.

items.title: Thirty-seven knobs, we can test one by one.
items.subtitle: Thirty-seven knobs, we can test one by one. But sixty million? How do you find which way to turn them all?

items.title: That's backpropagation, coming up next time.
items.subtitle: That's backpropagation, coming up next time.
